metaData.title: Masayoshi Son and Sam Altman: Why Are They Setting 'Sky-High' Prices for AI?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Starting from the high-valuation IPOs of companies like Zhipu AI, SpaceX, and Anthropic, this article analyzes the pricing logic of AI faith and warns of the liquidity shock from the July 2026 lock-up expiration wave.
metaData.summary: Set against the backdrop of a wave of AI company IPOs in the first half of 2026, the article explores why the market is willing to give extremely high valuations to AI companies that are not yet profitable. The author unpacks this from three perspectives: 'scarcity premium,' 'industry substitution potential,' and 'the formula of AI faith.' It begins with Zhipu AI as an example, using limit calculations for three market pools—AI Coding, SaaS substitution, and content production—to show that its valuation has already priced in the rewriting of R&D and software budgets across the entire application layer. It then uses Masayoshi Son's SoftBank as a case study to demonstrate how a vertically integrated path from Arm chips to OpenAI gains market recognition. Finally, it focuses on the lock-up expiration wave for Zhipu AI and MiniMax in July 2026, pointing out that the circulating supply could expand several-fold to tenfold, directly challenging the 'scarcity premium.' The article also compares the 2000 internet bubble with the current AI investment frenzy, concluding that AI companies have real revenue and are backed by tech giants, but their capital expenditure as a percentage of revenue has already surpassed the peak levels of the telecom bubble.

mainPoints.point: The core logic behind high AI valuations is the 'scarcity premium' and 'industry substitution potential.'
mainPoints.explanation: Pure-play AI unicorns are the sexiest capital narrative of 2026, with extremely small circulating supply and overwhelming capital demand, pushing prices to levels where traditional valuation models fall silent. Meanwhile, the market is pricing in the rewriting of R&D, software, and content production budgets by AI.

mainPoints.point: Masayoshi Son's SoftBank is the best lens for understanding the pricing of AI faith.
mainPoints.explanation: Through vertical integration from Arm (chip design) to Ampere (computing chips) to Stargate (data centers) to OpenAI (model layer), SoftBank has built a causal chain from underlying silicon to top-level intelligence, earning extremely high valuation rewards from the market.

mainPoints.point: The July 2026 lock-up expiration wave will directly test the sustainability of AI faith.
mainPoints.explanation: After the lock-up periods for Zhipu AI and MiniMax expire, the circulating supply could expand several-fold to tenfold. With current stock prices far above the IPO price, shareholders have strong incentives to cash out their massive paper gains, putting pressure on the 'scarcity premium' pricing factor.

mainPoints.point: The current AI investment frenzy differs fundamentally from the 2000 internet bubble, but risks are still accumulating.
mainPoints.explanation: AI companies have real and rapidly growing revenue and are backed by tech giants, so a dot-com-style mass extinction is unlikely. However, the capital expenditure-to-revenue ratio for giants like Meta and Microsoft has already surpassed the peak levels of the telecom bubble, indicating accumulating risks.

keyQuotes: The market is pricing in the rewriting of R&D, software, and content production budgets by the entire AI application layer.
Masayoshi Son's 'revenge' path is the best lens for understanding the pricing of this AI faith.
When the circulating supply expands from 3% to over 50%, the magic of the 'scarcity premium' pricing factor will diminish.

What we should really worry about is whether these trillion-dollar valuations can truly hold. If any one company's stock price breaks below its IPO price, the impact on the valuation anchor of the entire AI sector would be far more devastating than a $200 billion liquidity loss.

relatedArticles.title: Why Did Hermes Take Over from OpenClaw in Just Two Months?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth comparison between the rising open-source AI Agent star Hermes and its predecessor OpenClaw, arguing that Hermes' success stems not from functional superiority but from encapsulating decision complexity—such as skill auto-evolution and proactive memory management—within underlying deterministic rules. This engineering safety net allowed it to deliver an automated 'gets better with use' experience precisely when the underlying technology was just barely sufficient.
